query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with a small amount of silver (Ag) will enable the in situ formation of a continuous, self‐lubricating tribolayer that sustains low friction and suppresses wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with a uniform microstructure and no additional soft phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor silver phase (approximately 5–10 at.%) into the alloy by alloying during powder synthesis or melting.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests in air using a ball‐on‐disk setup under moderate to high contact loads over a temperature range from ambient (≈25 °C) to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and dynamic evolution of Ag‐rich precipitates that migrate to the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, finely dispersed Ag precipitates act as a soft phase reducing shear strength at the contact interface. At elevated temperatures, increased Ag diffusivity causes these precipitates to coalesce and form an adherent, continuous Ag-rich tribolayer that minimizes metal–metal contact, limits oxidation‐induced abrasive wear, and thereby maintains a low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the Ag-modified material is predicted to show a notably lower steady-state friction coefficient (roughly 20–30% lower) and a wear rate reduced by potentially an order of magnitude over the entire temperature range tested.
generation.baseline: The CoCrFeNi alloy in its unmodified state, which under sliding exhibits inconsistent lubrication with increased friction and wear—especially at high temperatures due to inadequate tribo‐protection.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under dry sliding conditions in atmospheric air, with contact pressures and sliding velocities similar to those in typical ball–on–disk tests, spanning temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: While reactive tribolayer formation via Ag has been demonstrated in related reactive wear protection systems (e.g., in TiNbZr–Ag alloys as shown in PMC8448869) and microalloying has improved wear resistance in similar HEA systems (e.g., PMC11643733), the temperature-dependent kinetics of Ag diffusion and the stability of the Ag-rich tribolayer in a CoCrFeNi matrix over such a wide temperature range remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi and one set doped with 5–10 at.% Ag by identical processing routes. Subject both sets to ball‐on‐disk sliding tests in air at three representative temperatures (e.g., 25 °C, 400 °C, and 800 °C) under equal loads. Post-test, characterize the friction coefficient and wear volume, and analyze the worn surfaces via SEM/EDS and XRD to verify the presence and continuity of any Ag-rich tribolayer.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (steady-state value at each temperature)
Wear rate (using 3D profilometry and mass loss measurements)
Surface microstructure and chemical composition (via SEM/EDS)
Phase identification of the tribolayer (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ag-doped samples do not consistently exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction (less than ~15% lower than baseline) and wear rate (less than ~50% reduction) across all temperatures, or if microstructural analysis fails to show the formation of a continuous Ag-rich tribolayer at the sliding interface, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals.
